observation.visible_scene: A bright, near-white surface holding about nine glossy colored spheres (two red, two green, two blue, two yellow, one orange), each casting a soft gray shadow on the surface. The spheres are arranged loosely: a row of red/green/blue near the top edge, an orange and a blue in the middle, a yellow lower-left, and a yellow plus a red on the right side.
visible_changes: The whole cluster of spheres slowly and continuously translates/rotates across the frame from the first to the last sample (e.g., the top-left red sphere drifts rightward and upward toward the top edge, the right-side yellow and red spheres drift outward/rightward, the middle orange and yellow spheres shift downward), consistent with a slow camera pan/rotation or scene rotation rather than individual ballistic motion.

Several spheres visibly deform over the excerpt rather than merely translating: the top red sphere flattens into an oblate/teardrop blob around the middle frames and then rounds again; the top-left green sphere shows a lumpy, jagged surface deformation; the middle blue sphere shows dents and a squashed silhouette; the right yellow and bottom-right red spheres alternately squash and stretch.
The shadows on the surface shift and change shape in step with the moving/deforming spheres, indicating the lighting and the spheres' positions are changing together.
The motion is ongoing at both crop boundaries; no start, stop, landing, or disappearance is shown.
outside_clip_unknowns: The cause of the deformations (impact, squeezing, or a soft-body simulation) is not shown.
What precedes the first frame and what follows the last frame (whether the drift continues or reverses, whether deformations settle) is unknown.
The exact number of spheres outside the cropped view and any off-screen contacts are unknown.
uncertain_details: Whether the global translation is camera movement or actual scene rotation cannot be fully separated; the background provides only weak cues.
The apparent 'jagged' edges on some deformed spheres may be rendering/anti-aliasing artifacts rather than true surface tearing.
The precise direction of the slow drift (slight clockwise vs counter-clockwise component) is hard to fix given the small per-frame changes.
